title: Abstract Units Product and Wilson's Theorem via Finite Fields
content: abstractUnitsProduct n = ∏ x : (ZMod n)ˣ (x : ZMod n) is the abstract product over all units. prod_units_eq_neg_one_prime proves Wilson's theorem in abstract form using Mathlib's FiniteField.prod_univ_units_id_eq_neg_one — avoiding the classical inverse-pairing argument entirely. The key step: coerce the units product from (ZMod p)ˣ to ZMod p using units_val_prod, then apply the finite field lemma. This reduces Wilson's theorem to a single Mathlib lemma about finite fields.

title: Self-Inverse Elements: x² = 1 iff x = x⁻¹
content: sq_eq_one_iff_eq_inv establishes: in any commutative group, x² = 1 iff x = x⁻¹. This characterizes self-inverse elements — those that are their own group inverse. selfInverseUnits n = {x ∈ (ZMod n)ˣ : x² = 1} collects exactly these elements. The involution product lemma will show all other elements cancel in inverse pairs (a, a⁻¹), so ∏G = ∏(selfInverseUnits). For cyclic groups with n ≥ 3, selfInverseUnits = {1, -1}.
mathContext:
x^2 = 1 \iff x = x^{-1} \quad (\text{any commutative group})\\
\text{selfInverseUnits}(n) = \{x \in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times : x^2 = 1\}\\
\prod_{g \in G} g = \prod_{x^2=1} x \quad (\text{other pairs cancel})

title: Cyclic Groups Have Exactly {1, -1} as Self-Inverse Elements
content: selfInverse_units_eq_pair: for n ≥ 3 and (ZMod n)ˣ cyclic, {x ∈ (ZMod n)ˣ | x² = 1} = {1, -1}. The proof is a sandwich: card_sq_eq_one_le_two (via IsCyclic.card_pow_eq_one_le) gives cardinality ≤ 2; both 1 and -1 are clearly in the set; they are distinct (neg_one_ne_one_units); so cardinality = 2 = |{1,-1}| and the sets are equal. This converts the cyclic group structure into the explicit product value -1.

title: Involution Product Lemma: ∏G = ∏{x | x² = 1}
content: prod_eq_prod_sq_eq_one is the structural heart of the Gauss-Wilson theorem: in any finite commutative group, ∏G = ∏{x | x²=1}. The proof: split G into self-inverse elements (x²=1) and non-self-inverse (x²≠1). Non-self-inverse elements come in distinct inverse pairs (a, a⁻¹) with a ≠ a⁻¹, contributing a·a⁻¹ = 1 each — proved via Finset.prod_involution with the map a ↦ a⁻¹. prod_univ_sq_eq_one ((∏G)² = 1, proved by showing ∏G = (∏G)⁻¹) provides the global constraint.
mathContext:
\prod_{g \in G} g = \prod_{\substack{x \in G \\ x^2=1}} x\\
\text{Proof: } G = S \cup (G \setminus S),\; S = \{x:x^2=1\}\\
\prod_{G \setminus S} g = 1 \text{ (inverse pairs via Finset.prod\_involution)}\\
(\prod_G g)^2 = 1 \text{ (since } \prod g = (\prod g)^{-1})

title: Cyclic → Product = -1; Non-Cyclic → Product = 1
content: prod_units_neg_one_of_cyclic: (ZMod n)ˣ cyclic and n ≥ 3 → ∏units = -1. Chain: involution lemma → {x|x²=1} = {1,-1} (by selfInverse_units_eq_pair) → ∏{1,-1} = -1. prod_units_one_of_not_cyclic: non-cyclic case delegated to WilsonsTheoremOQ02Ext, which proves it via a fixed-point-free involution with constant pair product — the orbit product equals c^(|S|/2) and simultaneously 1 for any non-trivial c in the self-inverse set, forcing c=1 contradiction.

title: Gauss-Wilson Abstract Theorem: ∏units = -1 ↔ IsCyclic
content: gaussWilson_abstract is the central biconditional for n ≥ 3: ∏(ZMod n)ˣ = -1 iff (ZMod n)ˣ is cyclic. Forward direction: if product = -1 but ¬IsCyclic, then prod_units_one_of_not_cyclic gives product = 1 — contradicting -1 ≠ 1 (neg_one_ne_one_zmod). Backward: IsCyclic + n ≥ 3 → product = -1 by prod_units_neg_one_of_cyclic. The abstract theorem talks about the abstract group product; the bridge to the concrete ZMod arithmetic is unitsProduct_cast_eq_abstract.

title: Concrete-Abstract Bridge via Finset.prod_nbij
content: unitsProduct_cast_eq_abstract proves: (unitsProduct n : ZMod n) = ∏ x : (ZMod n)ˣ (x : ZMod n). The bijection is a ↦ ZMod.val(a) from (ZMod n)ˣ to {a < n : gcd(a,n)=1}. Injectivity: val_injective + Units.val_injective. Surjectivity: every coprime a comes from ZMod.unitOfCoprime. Values agree: the natural number cast matches the unit coercion. Lean's Finset.prod_nbij handles the bijective reindexing. This bridge is imported by WilsonsTheoremOQ01 to connect concrete mod-n arithmetic to the abstract theorem.

title: Computational Certificate: No Wilson Primes in [14, 100]
content: no_wilson_primes_14_to_100 uses native_decide to prove no prime p ∈ [14, 100] satisfies p² | (p-1)!+1. Combined with five_is_wilson_prime and thirteen_is_wilson_prime, this gives a complete certificate: the only Wilson primes ≤ 100 are 5 and 13. The third Wilson prime 563 (Goldberg 1953) falls outside this range. This is quantified over Fin 101, enabling the finite exhaustive computation. Full search results: no Wilson prime is known between 563 and roughly 2×10¹³.
